title: Module 4 Misconception Sort
intro: Decide whether each statement is true, false, or depends. These are the misconceptions that cost students points on exams.

items.s: A negative z score means the data point is wrong or impossible.
items.why: A negative z simply marks a score below the mean.

items.s: Converting scores to z scores makes a skewed distribution normal.
items.why: Standardizing is a linear transformation. The shape stays exactly the same.

items.s: A z score of +1.50 on one test and +1.50 on another test mean the same relative standing in each group.
items.why: Each z is measured against its own distribution, so both scores sit 1.5 SDs above their group mean.

items.s: The proportion above z = +1.00 equals the proportion below z = −1.00 in a normal distribution.
The probability of any exact single score in a continuous distribution is large.
items.why: For a continuous variable, the area at a single point is zero. Probabilities are for ranges of scores.

items.s: You can use the Unit Normal Table for any distribution.
items.why: The table applies only to normal distributions. For skewed data the proportions will be wrong.

items.s: Whether the body or the tail column answers a question about the proportion above a positive z
items.why: For a positive z, the area above is the tail. For a negative z, the area above is the body. Sketch the curve first.

items.s: A raw score of 70 on one test beats a raw score of 60 on a different test.
items.why: It depends on each test's mean and SD. A 70 against a mean of 80 and SD of 5 has z = −2, while a 60 against a mean of 50 and SD of 5 has z = +2.
